heading: Rust, Go and C# on the web
body: A service written only in Rust, only in Go or only in C# needs no browser sibling on the web. Rust links on the three desktops, C# links on Windows, and Go links on no host. Where a host links the service, it runs natively. Everywhere else, including the web, it runs as WebAssembly: in the browser, or in the web view of a native target (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045; an ADR is an architecture decision record). Rust compiles with rustc --target wasm32-unknown-unknown into one small module. Go compiles into one module for all the Go services of the application. A release build compiles it with TinyGo, which leaves out most of the Go runtime, so a small service is about 300 KB (100 KB as sent with Brotli). Without TinyGo, or when TinyGo cannot compile the services, the standard Go compiler (GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm) builds a module that carries the whole Go runtime and starts at about 2.7 MB. The page loads the module with the wasm_exec.js of the compiler that built it (see WebAssembly compilers per language, ADR 0081). C# publishes onto the .NET browser runtime. That runtime is about 3 MB, and the service worker caches it once. F# services compile into a small F# library that runs on the same .NET browser runtime, so a page with C# and F# services loads that runtime once; no host links F#, so an F# service runs as WebAssembly on every target, Windows included (ADR 0073). So when a service has several of these versions, Tachyon uses Rust, then Go, then C#, then F#. The page speaks the same companion protocol as a native host, so the service is the same file. Its fields render. Its methods take JSON arguments: String, &str, bool, numbers or TacValue in Rust, string, bool, numbers, slices, maps or structs in Go, and string, bool, numbers or object in C# and F#. An F# service shows its `member val` properties and its public members. A view reaches the exported Go members with a lower-case first letter, so Count is {tally.count}. Service and NeedsAll sit on their own lines above the type. Rust spells Service as #[Service], Go spells it as // @Service, C# spells it as [Service], and F# spells it as [<Service>]. A bare constructor lets every field take the property with the same name, and it makes the service one per component. A WebAssembly service has no DOM and no platform. It is state and logic over the properties its tag passes. Those properties may carry a data file: the start-up request may carry up to 1 MiB (1048576 bytes) in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin and Ruby. Every later request, such as a method call, may carry up to 64 KiB (65536 bytes). A bigger request fails, and the error names the service, the size and the limit, for example: Web service documentation: The request is 1072202 bytes. The limit is 1048576 bytes. Pass less data to the service. A method call names the method too: The request to add is 70121 bytes. ty doctor checks for the wasm32-unknown-unknown target, Go 1.27 and the .NET wasm-tools workload. It also lists TinyGo and Binaryen's wasm-opt as optional tools: release builds use them to make the modules smaller.
